mission: CHAI is a UC Berkeley research group led by Stuart Russell that wants to re-found AI on 'provably beneficial' principles. Instead of machines that maximise a fixed objective, it studies AI that is uncertain about what humans want and so defers to us and can be switched off. It develops theory, runs experiments, educates the public and advises on policy.

key_work.title: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning (CIRL)
key_work.plain_summary: Frames AI alignment as a game where a robot and a human share the human's goal, but only the human knows it — so the robot must learn what we want by watching and asking.

key_work.title: The Off-Switch Game
key_work.plain_summary: Shows that an AI that is uncertain about our preferences has a reason to let us switch it off, while a certain one does not.

key_work.title: Inverse Reward Design
key_work.plain_summary: Treats the reward a designer writes as evidence about what they really want, so an agent behaves cautiously in situations the designer did not anticipate.

key_work.title: Adversarial Policies: Attacking Deep Reinforcement Learning
key_work.plain_summary: Shows that trained AI agents can be beaten by opponents that act in strange, seemingly random ways — a warning about how brittle learned behaviour can be.

key_work.title: An unexamined cause of the OpenAI Hugging Face hacking incident: its binary performance metric
key_work.plain_summary: A CHAI post arguing that grading an AI system on a simple pass/fail metric contributed to a real-world hacking incident, illustrating how optimising a proxy goes wrong.

funding_note: Sponsors listed on CHAI's About page: Open Philanthropy, the Future of Life Institute, the Leverhulme Trust and CITRIS.

people.role: Founder; Professor of EECS, UC Berkeley
CHAI PhD alumnus; co-author of CIRL and the Off-Switch Game (now MIT)

warnings.text: Current AI maximises a proxy for value — clicks, dollars, correct predictions — and no one knows how to turn 'be good for humanity' into an optimisation problem.
Machines far more capable than humans could pursue objectives with negative and perhaps irreversible outcomes.
An AI that is certain of a fixed objective has an incentive to resist being switched off.

recommendations.text: Refocus AI research away from achieving arbitrary objectives and toward provably beneficial behaviour.
Build AI that is uncertain about human preferences and learns them by observing and deferring to people.
Bring in social science, law, philosophy and economics, since 'beneficial' depends on human properties.
